content: The common cold is a widespread illness that, while generally mild and self-limiting, leads to numerous visits to primary care providers and significant absences from work or school. Current treatments for cold symptoms offer limited effectiveness. Corticosteroids, known for their anti-inflammatory properties, are effective in treating other upper respiratory tract infections, and it has been hypothesized that they might also be beneficial for the common cold. This updated review includes one additional study to evaluate this hypothesis. The objective of this review was to compare the effects of corticosteroids with standard care for the common cold, focusing on symptom resolution and improvement in both children and adults. To gather evidence, researchers searched multiple databases, including the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), the Database of Reviews of Effects (DARE), the NHS Health Economics Database, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to May 2015. The inclusion criteria were randomized, double-blind, controlled trials that compared corticosteroids to either placebo or standard clinical management. Two independent reviewers extracted data and assessed the quality of the trials. Due to the limited and heterogeneous nature of the data, a meta-analysis could not be performed, and the findings are presented as a narrative summary. Three trials involving a total of 353 participants were included in the review. Two trials compared intranasal corticosteroids to placebo, while one trial compared intranasal corticosteroids to usual care. None of the trials investigated the use of oral corticosteroids. In the two placebo-controlled trials, intranasal corticosteroids did not demonstrate any significant benefit in reducing the duration or severity of cold symptoms. In one trial with 54 participants, the average number of symptomatic days was 10.3 in the placebo group and 10.7 in the corticosteroid group, with no statistically significant difference (P = 0.72). Another trial with 199 participants also found no significant differences in symptom duration between the corticosteroid and placebo groups. The overall risk of bias in these two trials was assessed as low or unclear. The third trial, which was single-blind and involved children aged 2 to 14 years who were also receiving oral antibiotics, had significant limitations in reporting outcome measures related to symptom resolution. This trial showed a high risk of bias. However, it reported that mean symptom severity scores were significantly lower in the group receiving intranasal corticosteroids in addition to oral amoxicillin. One placebo-controlled trial investigated the presence of rhinovirus in nasal aspirates and found no differences between the corticosteroid and placebo groups. Only one of the three trials reported on adverse events, and no differences were observed between groups. Two trials reported secondary bacterial infections, with one case of sinusitis and one case of acute otitis media, both occurring in the corticosteroid groups. Due to the lack of comparable outcome measures across the studies, the data could not be pooled for analysis. In conclusion, the current evidence does not support the use of intranasal corticosteroids for relieving symptoms of the common cold. However, the evidence base is limited, with only three trials included, one of which was of very poor quality. The overall statistical power of the findings is low. Further large-scale, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials in both adults and children are necessary to provide a definitive answer to this question.
